m: The word “politarch” is rare in literature, and Luke is the main writer to use it. Acts 17:6, 8 says the mob dragged Jason and others before the politarchs. The finds show that Luke used the right title for a Macedonian city. Paul praises “the churches of Macedonia,” which included Thessalonica, for giving out of “deep poverty” (2 Corinthians 8:1-2). Philippians 4:16 says the Philippians sent help to Paul “even while I was in Thessalonica,” and sent it more than once. Colossians 4:10 sends greetings from Aristarchus, Paul’s “fellow prisoner,” who came from Thessalonica (Acts 20:4; 27:2). In 1 Thessalonians 2:14 Paul says the believers suffered “from your own countrymen” the things the churches of Judea suffered. The magistrates who heard the charge against Jason in Acts 17:6-9 are the city officials the letters have in mind when they speak of pressure on the church.
c: The inscription lists six politarchs and dates to the 2nd century AD, about a century after Paul. The office is older: Thessalonica had politarchs in the time of Augustus.
r: Acts 17:1-9; Acts 20:4; 2 Corinthians 8:1-5; Philippians 4:15-16; Colossians 4:10; 1 Thessalonians 1:1; 1 Thessalonians 2:14; 2 Thessalonians 1:4

n: Berea (Veria)
w: A stone platform in the town, called the Bema, honors Paul’s preaching, with a mosaic from 1960. Remnants of the old Jewish quarter lie near the river.
m: The Bereans received the word “with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily” (17:11).
c: The Bema is a memorial, and the town has few first-century remains.

n: The Areopagus and the Acropolis
w: The Areopagus is a rocky hill north-west of the Acropolis. Stone benches are cut into the hill, and a bronze plaque with Acts 17:22-31 in Greek was fixed to the rock in 1964.
m: Acts 17:19 says the philosophers “took him and brought him to the Areopagus,” which may mean the council that met there or the hill itself. First Thessalonians 3:1 says that Paul was “left on our own in Athens,” which is the time of his speech on the Areopagus in Acts 17.
c: In Paul’s day the council may have met in the Royal Stoa in the Agora.

n: The Athenian Agora: philosophers and altars
w: The marketplace has the rebuilt Stoa of Attalos, the Altar of the Twelve Gods, the Stoa Poikile where the Stoics met, and the Temple of Hephaistos. Greek writers record altars “to unknown gods” in Athens, and an altar fragment from Pergamum carries the same words.
m: Acts 17:16-21 says Paul reasoned “in the marketplace every day” with Epicurean and Stoic philosophers. His speech quotes the Greek poets (17:28; the line “we are his offspring” is from Aratus). In 1 Thessalonians 3:1-2 Paul says that he waited in Athens and sent Timothy to Thessalonica from there.
c: No altar reading “To the unknown god” (singular) has been found in Athens.

n: Corinth: the city Paul stayed in
w: The excavated city has the Temple of Apollo, a large agora with shops, a platform called the Bema where officials judged, the Peirene fountain, and a stone meat market. A carved lintel reading “[Syna]gogue of the Hebr[ews]” was found nearby, though it is probably later.
m: Paul spent eighteen months in Corinth (Acts 18:11) and was brought “before the judgment seat” (bema) of Gallio (18:12). The shops in the agora fit the tentmaking work he shared with Aquila and Priscilla (18:3). In 2 Corinthians Paul writes to the church he founded here, tells of a painful second visit (2:1), and says he is coming “a third time” (12:14). Most readers think Paul wrote 1 and 2 Thessalonians from Corinth, since Silas and Timothy joined him there (Acts 18:5) and both are named in the greetings (1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:1). Second Timothy 4:20 says, “Erastus has remained at Corinth.” The city was where Paul had stayed longest after Ephesus, and the letter gives no reason for Erastus’ stay there.
c: The Bema is large enough to be the tribunal for the Gallio story, but Acts does not describe it. The lintel is probably later than Paul.
r: Acts 18:1-18; Acts 19:1; Romans 16:21-23; 1 Corinthians 1:2; 1 Corinthians 2:1-5; 2 Corinthians 1:1; 2 Corinthians 2:1; 2 Corinthians 13:1; 1 Thessalonians 3:6; 2 Thessalonians 3:17; 2 Timothy 4:20

n: The Erastus pavement at Corinth
w: A paving block near the theater is carved in Latin: “Erastus, in return for his aedileship, laid [this pavement] at his own expense.”
m: Paul sends greetings to “Erastus, the city treasurer” (Romans 16:23), and Acts 19:22 names an Erastus among his helpers. The pavement shows that a man of that name held office in Corinth. Second Timothy 4:20 says, “Erastus has remained at Corinth.” The letter does not say whether this is the city official of the pavement or the helper of Acts 19:22, and Erastus was a common name.
c: Erastus was a common name. Scholars debate whether this man is the Erastus of Romans, and whether an aedile and a treasurer were the same office.

n: The Gallio inscription at Delphi
w: Fragments of a letter from the emperor Claudius, carved at Delphi, name “Junius Gallio, my friend and proconsul” of Achaia. It dates to Claudius’s 26th acclamation, in the first half of AD 52.
m: Acts 18:12 says that “when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia” the Jews brought Paul before him. The letter gives one of the few fixed dates in Paul’s life: Gallio served about AD 51-52, so Paul reached Corinth in about AD 50-51. The Gallio inscription helps date Paul’s stay in Corinth, where Timothy came back with the news that led to 1 Thessalonians (3:6; Acts 18:5, 12). That puts the letter in about AD 50-51 and makes it one of the earliest of Paul’s letters.
c: The inscription fixes when Gallio ruled, not when Paul stood before him; the exact year of the hearing is inferred.

n: Cenchreae, the eastern harbor of Corinth
w: Excavations (1963-68) uncovered harbor warehouses, now partly under the sea, and a shrine of Isis with colored glass panels. The harbor served Corinth’s east side toward Ephesus.
m: Paul “cut his hair, for he was under a vow” before sailing from Cenchreae (Acts 18:18). Paul also commends Phoebe, a deacon of the church there (Romans 16:1).
c: No Christian building from Paul’s day has been found at Cenchreae.

n: The edict of Claudius and the Jews of Rome
w: The Roman historian Suetonius says Claudius “expelled the Jews from Rome, since they were constantly rioting at the instigation of Chrestus.” A papyrus letter from Claudius to the Alexandrians (AD 41) also warns Jews not to stir up trouble.
m: Acts 18:2 says Aquila and Priscilla had “recently come from Italy because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome.” Many link Suetonius’s “Chrestus” to disputes over Christ. Some scholars link the early troubles that Hebrews recalls (10:32-34), when the readers were publicly abused, and had their property seized, to the expulsion of Jews from Rome under Claudius in about AD 49. The letter does not say where its readers lived, so the link is a guess.
c: The date of the expulsion is debated: the Christian writer Orosius gave AD 49, but others place it earlier.

n: The Great Theater at Ephesus
per: Hellenistic, enlarged in the 1st-2nd centuries AD
w: The theater is cut into the slope of Mount Pion and held about 24,000 people. A marble street (the Arcadian Way) ran from it to the harbor.
m: The riot in Acts 19:23-41 ends in this theater, with the crowd “rushing together” as Paul’s companions Gaius and Aristarchus are dragged in. The crowd chants “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” for two hours. Paul’s “burden far beyond our ability to endure” in Asia (2 Corinthians 1:8) may refer to the troubles that ended in this theater, though the letter does not say. The crowd in the theater chanted for two hours (Acts 19:34). Years later the church in the same city received a letter that tells its members to “make your stand against the devil’s schemes” (Ephesians 6:11). First Timothy 1:20 names an Alexander at Ephesus whom Paul “handed over to Satan.” Acts 19:33 has another Alexander in this theater during the riot, and 2 Timothy 4:14 has an Alexander the coppersmith. The letters do not say whether these are one man or several. Second Timothy 4:14-15 warns of “Alexander the coppersmith,” who “vigorously opposed our message.” The letter does not say whether he was the Alexander of Acts 19:33.
c: The present seating was built or finished after Paul’s time, but a theater stood on the site.
r: Acts 19:21-41; Acts 20:1; 1 Corinthians 15:32; 1 Corinthians 16:8-9; 2 Corinthians 1:8-10; Ephesians 6:10-20; 1 Timothy 1:20; 2 Timothy 4:14-15

n: The Temple of Artemis
per: 6th century BC; rebuilt in the 4th century BC
w: The temple of Artemis was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, four times the size of the Parthenon. It was found in 1869-74 by J. T. Wood in a marsh near the town. Only the foundations and one reconstructed column survive.
m: Acts 19:27 calls Artemis “the goddess” worshiped by “all Asia and the world,” and the town clerk says Ephesus is the “temple keeper” of the great Artemis (19:35). Most of the first readers of Ephesians lived in the city of this temple. Ephesians speaks of “rule and authority, power and dominion” (1:21) and of “the rulers,” “the authorities” and “the powers of this world’s darkness” (6:12). Nothing in the letter names Artemis, but her city knew a world of unseen powers. First Timothy 3:15 calls the church “the pillar and foundation of the truth,” at a city whose great temple had over a hundred marble columns. Paul’s instructions to women in 2:9-15 were given in a city where Artemis was worshiped, a goddess served by priestesses and priests, and some scholars read the passage against that background. Others do not, and the letter does not mention the goddess. The last words of 1 John, “keep yourselves from idols” (5:21), do not name the temple of Artemis, and readers differ on whether the idols are images or false ideas of God; the temple would still have stood beside the first readers.
c: The temple was destroyed in the 3rd and 4th centuries AD.
r: Acts 19:23-41; 1 Corinthians 3:16-17; Ephesians 2:1-3; Ephesians 3:10; Ephesians 6:12; 1 Timothy 2:9-15; 1 Timothy 3:15; 1 John 5:21

n: The silversmiths of Ephesus
w: Inscriptions from Ephesus mention guilds of silversmiths and a man named Demetrius who served as a “temple warden” for Artemis. Small terracotta and stone figures of Artemis are common finds at Ephesus.
m: Acts 19:24 says “a silversmith named Demetrius” made silver shrines of Artemis and his trade was hurt by Paul’s preaching, which started the riot.
c: No inscription can be tied to the Demetrius of Acts, and few silver shrines survive.

n: The “Ephesian Letters” and the magic books
pl: Ephesus and the Greek magical papyri
w: Ancient writers speak of the Ephesia grammata, six mysterious words said to protect the user. Collections of magical papyri from Egypt contain spells, charms and curses, and show that magic books were bought and sold.
m: Acts 19:19 says believers in Ephesus burned their books of magic, worth “fifty thousand pieces of silver.” The scene shows how common magic was in the city. Paul’s list of “the acts of the flesh” includes “idolatry and sorcery” (Galatians 5:20), and people in Asia Minor could turn to charms and spell books. Ephesians 2:2 speaks of “the ruler of the power of the air,” and 6:12 of “the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms.” A city that bought charms and spell books would have understood why Paul speaks of struggling with such powers. Colossians 2:8 warns against teaching based on “the spiritual forces of the world,” and 2:15 speaks of “the powers and authorities.” Ephesus, the leading city of the province, was known for charms and spell books, which shows the world in which people looked for protection from such powers. Whether the teachers at Colossae used magic is not known.
c: The Ephesian Letters are known from writers later than Paul. No book burned by the believers has been found.
r: Acts 19:11-20; Galatians 5:19-21; Ephesians 2:2; Ephesians 6:12; Colossians 2:8; Colossians 2:15

n: Miletus: the port of the elders’ farewell
w: Miletus had four harbors, a large theater, the Delphinion (the sanctuary of Apollo) and baths. The harbor has since silted up, leaving the site inland. A pair of marble lions stood beside the main harbor.
m: Paul stopped here instead of Ephesus to save time and called the elders of Ephesus to him (Acts 20:16-17). It was about 50 km (30 miles) by road. Paul told the elders at Miletus, “Be shepherds of the church of God,” and warned that “savage wolves will come in among you” (Acts 20:28-29). Ephesians 4:11 lists “pastors and teachers” among Christ’s gifts to the church. Second Timothy 4:20 says, “Trophimus I left sick in Miletus.” Acts 20:4 and 21:29 show Trophimus, from Asia, going with Paul to Jerusalem, so the stop in 2 Timothy must belong to a later journey.
c: Most standing remains are later than Paul. Acts does not describe the buildings.

n: God-fearers: inscriptions from Aphrodisias and Miletus
w: A large stone from Aphrodisias lists Jewish donors and a group of “God-fearers” (theosebeis). A seat in the theater at Miletus is marked “place of the Jews, who are also God-fearers.”
m: Luke often names Gentiles who worshiped the God of Israel without full conversion: Cornelius (10:2), and the “devout Greeks” in Antioch, Thessalonica, Athens and Corinth (13:16, 26; 17:4, 17; 18:7). Inscriptions show non-Jews who worshiped with the synagogue without being circumcised. In Galatians 2:3 Titus, “a Greek,” was not compelled to be circumcised, and chapter 5 argues against requiring it of Gentile believers. Ephesians 2:11-13 reminds Gentiles that they were once “separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of the promise,” and have “been brought near through the blood of Christ.” God-fearers stood near the synagogue without being fully inside it. Acts 17:4 says that in Thessalonica “a large number of God-fearing Greeks” joined Paul and Silas. First Thessalonians 1:9 describes the church as people who “turned to God from idols,” which suggests that many were Gentiles who had not been part of the synagogue.
c: The inscriptions are later than Paul, and scholars still discuss how the term was used.
r: Acts 10:2; Acts 13:16; Acts 13:26; Acts 17:4; Acts 18:7; Galatians 2:3; Galatians 5:2-6; Ephesians 2:11-13; 1 Thessalonians 1:9

n: Antipatris
w: Herod rebuilt Aphek by the springs of the Yarkon River and named it for his father Antipater. A stretch of Roman road with milestones leads from it to Caesarea. A Turkish fort (Binar Bashi) now stands on the mound.
m: The soldiers brought Paul from Jerusalem by night as far as Antipatris (Acts 23:31), then the horsemen went on to Caesarea the next day.
c: The fort and most of what you see is later than Paul.

n: Felix, the governor, and his coins
w: Antonius Felix issued bronze coins in AD 54 with palm branches and shields, honoring Claudius and Agrippina. Tacitus says he “wielded royal power with the spirit of a slave.” He married Drusilla, daughter of Agrippa I.
m: Acts 24:22-27 shows Felix as well informed about “the Way,” frightened when Paul speaks of judgment, and hoping for a bribe. Drusilla sits beside him (24:24).
c: The coins show the governor and his years; they say nothing of Paul.

n: Festus and the coins of Nero
w: Porcius Festus issued bronze prutot dated to the fifth year of Nero (AD 58/59) with Nero’s name and palm branches.
m: Acts 24:27 says Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus after two years. Paul appeals to Caesar (25:11), meaning the emperor Nero.
c: The date Festus began is debated, usually put between AD 55 and 60. The coins help but do not settle it.

n: King Agrippa II and Bernice
w: Agrippa II ruled territories in the north and renamed Banias “Neronias” for Nero. The ruins there include a large palace complex, and his coins carry his name and portraits of the emperors.
m: Acts 25:13-26:32 has Agrippa and his sister Bernice hear Paul in Caesarea, and Agrippa says “In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?”
c: The palace identification at Banias is uncertain. Agrippa also lived in the old Hasmonean palace in Jerusalem.

n: Myra and the grain ships
w: Myra has a theater and rock-cut tombs in the cliff. Its port, Andriake, has a large granary built under Hadrian in AD 129, long after Paul, used for Egyptian grain.
m: The centurion found “a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy” at Myra and put his prisoners on board (Acts 27:5-6). It shows the Egyptian grain route to Rome.
c: The granary is later than Paul, but it shows the port’s role.

n: Fair Havens, Crete
pl: Kaloi Limenes, south coast of Crete
w: The small bay called Kaloi Limenes (“Fair Havens”) keeps its Greek name on the south coast. A small chapel recalls the visit, and the ruins of ancient Lasea (27:8) lie to the east.
m: Paul warned that continuing would end in “disaster and great loss,” but the centurion trusted the pilot and the owner and sailed on (27:9-12). Paul’s letters name Crete only in Titus 1:5, where he says he left Titus on the island to “set in order what was unfinished.” Acts does not say Paul worked on Crete, so that visit is usually placed after Acts ends.
c: The bay was not a good place to winter, which is why the sailors wanted Phoenix.

n: Roman grain ships
pl: Wrecks found off France and Cyprus; harbors of Alexandria and Ostia
w: The wreck of the Madrague de Giens (about 40 m long, 1st century BC) shows how Roman merchants carried wine and other cargo in large ships. A painted merchant ship of the 3rd century AD, the Isis Giminiana, shows a freighter of a similar kind. Rome got much of its wheat from Egypt and North Africa, and ships from Alexandria carried the Egyptian share.
m: Acts 27:37 says there were 276 people on Paul’s ship, and Josephus says he sailed to Rome on a ship carrying about 600. The ship had a figurehead of “the Twin Brothers” (28:11). In 2 Corinthians 11:25 Paul says “three times I was shipwrecked,” before the wreck at Malta in Acts 27. Large ancient ships were steered by one or two big steering oars at the stern, which Acts 27:40 calls “rudders” (the Greek pedalion occurs in the New Testament only there and in James 3:4). James 3:4 pictures a ship driven by strong winds and turned by a very small rudder wherever the pilot wishes.
c: The wreck and the painting differ in age, and neither is Paul’s ship.

n: Malta: the island of the shipwreck
w: A bay on the north coast is called St Paul’s Bay. Four ancient anchors have been recovered nearby, and Greek inscriptions name the island’s chief official “first of the Maltese.” A Roman villa and a grotto honored as Paul’s lodging lie at Rabat.
m: Acts 28:1 says “we learned that the island was called Malta” (Melite), and 28:7 calls Publius “the chief man of the island,” a title matched by those inscriptions.
c: Other islands were also proposed for the wreck (Kefalonia, Mljet). The inscriptions fit the title but not the man.

n: Puteoli
w: Puteoli was the main port for the Egyptian grain fleet before Ostia was built. Remains include the market (called the Serapeum), docks and a large Flavian amphitheater, built later.
m: Paul found believers here who invited him to stay seven days (Acts 28:13-14), then walked to Rome by the Appian Way.
c: The amphitheater and much of the town are later than Paul.

n: The Appian Way
pl: Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns, south of Rome
w: The “queen of roads” ran from Rome to Brindisi. Long stretches of basalt paving and milestones can still be walked. Forum Appii lay 43 Roman miles from Rome; the Three Taverns about 33.
m: Acts 28:15 says believers from Rome met Paul at “the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns.” “When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage.”
c: The towns are known from Roman writers; no first-century church is found there.

n: Rome: Paul’s rented house and his tomb
per: AD 60-62; tradition of his death about AD 64-67
w: Roman writers record the Praetorian Guard, who held prisoners awaiting trial, and the camp where they lived. The basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls stands over a tomb honored as Paul’s; a sarcophagus inscribed “Paulo apostolo mart[yri]” lies beneath the altar.
m: Acts 28:16 says Paul was allowed to live by himself “with a soldier to guard him,” and Acts 28:30 adds he stayed two years in “his own rented house.” Ephesians calls Paul “the prisoner of Christ Jesus” (3:1; 4:1) and “an ambassador in chains” (6:20). If he wrote from Rome, he was under guard in a rented house for two years. If Philippians was written from Rome, Paul’s guards and “the household of Caesar” were all around him, and he says his chains had become known “throughout the whole palace guard” (1:13). Colossians 4:3 says the mystery of Christ is “for which I am in chains,” and the letter ends with “Remember my chains” (4:18). If it was written from Rome, Paul was under guard in a rented house for two years. Second Timothy shows Paul again a prisoner in Rome, in chains (1:16; 2:9) and expecting to die (4:6-8). Early writers such as the author of 1 Clement and Eusebius say that Paul was put to death at Rome. The letter itself does not describe the end. If Philemon was written from Rome, it comes from the years when Paul lived under guard in rented quarters and received visitors (Acts 28:16, 30-31). In the letter he calls himself “a prisoner of Christ Jesus” (verse 9) and says Onesimus could “minister to me in my chains” (verse 13).
c: The location of the rented house is unknown. The tomb is traditional, though the church has venerated it since the 4th century.
r: Acts 28:14-31; Romans 1:7-15; Ephesians 3:1; Ephesians 4:1; Ephesians 6:20; Philippians 1:12-14; Philippians 4:22; Colossians 4:3; Colossians 4:18; 2 Timothy 1:16-17; 2 Timothy 4:6-8; Philemon 1:9-13

n: The Roman Forum
per: 1st century BC to the 4th century AD
w: The valley between the Capitoline and Palatine hills where Rome’s law courts, temples and speakers’ platform stood. The paved square, the Rostra and the foundations of the Senate house and several temples can still be walked.
m: Paul writes to believers who lived in the city that the Forum stood for, with its law, its taxes and its claim to rule the world (Romans 1:7; 13:1-7). The Forum shows what “governing authorities” looked like to the people who first heard the letter. If “Babylon” in 1 Peter 5:13 is a name for Rome, the Forum is the heart of the city Peter has in mind, a capital that Revelation also calls Babylon (Revelation 17-18).
c: Most of the standing ruins date after Paul’s time, because of the fire of AD 64 and later building by the emperors. Few Christians would have lived in the Forum itself, which was a place of government and trade.

n: The Jewish inscriptions of Rome
pl: Jewish catacombs of Rome (Villa Torlonia, Monteverde and others)
w: Greek and Latin epitaphs in the Jewish catacombs name a number of separate congregations in Rome, such as the synagogues of the Augustesians, the Agrippesians, the Volumnesians and the Hebrews, and one called “of the Olive” (Elaia). Many tombs carry a menorah.
m: Romans is addressed to a city where Jews had lived for generations in many small congregations rather than one large body. That helps explain why Paul speaks to both Jewish and Gentile believers and why chapters 2, 9-11 and 14 take so much trouble over how they relate.
c: The inscriptions are later than Paul by at least a century, and the congregations may have formed in his day or afterward. The synagogue “of the Olive” is a name only and does not show a link with Romans 11.

n: The Altar of Augustan Peace
w: A marble altar enclosed by carved walls, ordered by the Senate to celebrate Augustus’s return from Spain and Gaul and the “Roman peace” he had brought. The walls show a procession of the imperial family, and a panel of Mother Earth with flowers and animals.
m: Paul says that those who are justified by faith “have peace with God” (Romans 5:1) and speaks of the God of peace (Romans 15:33; 16:20). Readers in Rome lived with another claim to bring peace, and the altar shows how plainly the empire stated it.
c: Paul does not mention the altar or the emperor’s peace by name. The contrast is one that modern readers draw, not something Romans states.

n: The Priene inscription: “the good news” of Augustus
pl: Priene, western Turkey (a copy is in the Berlin museum)
w: A decree of the cities of Asia to start the new year on the birthday of Augustus. It calls his birth “the beginning of the good news (euangelion) for the world” and names him savior.
m: Paul opens Romans by calling himself “set apart for the gospel of God” (Romans 1:1), and says he is not ashamed of it (1:16). The word “gospel” was already used in the Greek world for announcements of an emperor’s birth, victories and rule. Philippians 3:20 says “we eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ,” and 2:11 says that “every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.” Greek cities gave emperors titles such as savior, and Paul gives those words to Christ. Paul uses “gospel” (euangelion) in both Thessalonian letters, “our gospel” in 1 Thessalonians 1:5 and “the gospel of God” in 2:2, 8, 9. In a city that honored the emperors, the word had a rival use for “good news” about Caesar. First Timothy calls God “our Savior” (1:1; 2:3; 4:10) and Christ “our hope” (1:1). Emperors were also called “savior” in Asia, and the wording would have been heard against that background. Titus calls both God and Christ “Savior,” three times each (1:3-4; 2:10, 13; 3:4, 6). Greek cities gave rulers that title. Titus 2:11 and 3:4 also say that God’s grace and kindness “appeared,” a word used for the arrival of a king or a god. The same language of a divine savior whose birthday is good news for the world stands behind the claims that Revelation 13 calls blasphemous names.
c: The word euangelion also comes from Isaiah (40:9; 52:7; 61:1), which Paul quotes in Romans 10:15. Scholars debate how much weight each background carries.
r: Romans 1:1-5; Romans 1:16; Romans 10:15; Philippians 2:9-11; Philippians 3:20; 1 Thessalonians 1:5; 1 Thessalonians 2:2; 1 Timothy 1:1; 1 Timothy 2:3; 1 Timothy 4:10; Titus 1:3-4; Titus 2:10-13; Titus 3:4-6; Revelation 13:1

n: Roman slave collars
pl: Museo Nazionale Romano, Rome (found in Rome)
w: Bronze collars worn by runaway slaves. One reads, “Hold me, lest I flee, and return me to my master Viventius on the estate of Callistus.”
m: Paul calls himself a “servant of Christ Jesus” (Romans 1:1; the Greek word, doulos, means slave) and says believers “have been set free from sin and have become slaves to righteousness” (Romans 6:18). Slavery was common in Rome, and many of those Paul greets in chapter 16 have slave names. Galatians speaks often of slavery: “slaves to those who by nature are not gods” (4:8) and “a yoke of slavery” (5:1). Paul also says he bears “the marks of Jesus” on his body (6:17); some scholars compare these to the brands slaves carried, but that is debated. Ephesians 6:5-9 tells slaves to obey “with respect and fear and sincerity of heart” and masters to “give up your use of threats,” because “He who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no favoritism with Him.” The letter does not end slavery, but it puts the master under the same Lord. Philippians 1:1 calls Paul and Timothy “servants of Christ Jesus,” and 2:7 says that Christ took “the form of a servant.” The Greek word in both places is doulos, a slave. Colossians 3:22 to 4:1 speaks to slaves and to masters, and 4:9 names Onesimus, “our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you.” He is the Onesimus of the letter to Philemon (Philemon 10-16). A collar like these was made to bring a runaway back to his owner. First Timothy 6:1-2 speaks to “all who are under the yoke of slavery,” and to those with “believing masters.” Collars like these show how slaves were marked and returned to their owners. Titus 2:9-10 asks slaves not to steal but to show “all good faith,” so that they “adorn the teaching about God our Savior.” Collars like these show how closely slaves were watched. Philemon 10-18 is about a slave who is away from his owner. If Onesimus ran away, a collar like these is what a recaptured runaway might wear. Paul asks instead that Philemon receive him “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (verse 16). 1 Peter 2:18 addresses household slaves (the Greek oiketai) and tells them to submit to their masters “even to those who are unreasonable.” A slave who ran away risked the collar and the lash. Peter points to Christ, who suffered for them, “leaving you an example” (2:21).
c: The surviving collars are about 300 years later than Paul. They show the world of slavery in Rome but come from a later century.
r: Romans 1:1; Romans 6:16-22; Romans 16:3-15; 1 Corinthians 7:21-23; Galatians 4:1-9; Galatians 5:1; Galatians 6:17; Ephesians 6:5-9; Philippians 1:1; Philippians 2:7; Colossians 3:22-25; Colossians 4:1; Colossians 4:9; 1 Timothy 6:1-2; Titus 2:9-10; Philemon 1:10-18; 1 Peter 2:18-25

n: The Roman catacombs
pl: Along the roads outside Rome (Callixtus, Priscilla, Domitilla and others)
w: Underground burial galleries cut into soft volcanic rock outside the city walls. Christians, Jews and others buried their dead there in long rows of shelves, with painted rooms for family meetings.
m: Paul writes that believers were “buried with Him through baptism into death” so that they may “walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:3-4), and that nothing, “neither death nor life,” can separate believers from God’s love (8:38-39). The catacombs show how the church in Rome later remembered those words. First Thessalonians 4:13-14 speaks of believers who “sleep.” The Greek word for a cemetery, koimeterion, means a sleeping place, and the early Christian burial inscriptions often say that the dead person “rests in peace.”
c: The catacombs are about a century or more later than Romans. They do not show how Christians in Rome buried their dead in the 50s, and the old idea that they hid there from persecution is not supported.

n: The house church and baptistery at Dura-Europos
w: An ordinary house in a Roman border city, rebuilt as a church. A room has a stone basin under a canopy for baptisms, and wall paintings show the Good Shepherd and Christ healing the paralytic.
m: Paul says baptism joins believers to Christ’s death and resurrection (Romans 6:3-4). The Dura house is the oldest church building known, and it shows what the early house churches in Romans 16:5 could have looked like. Titus 3:5 says God saved us “through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.” Many readers hear baptism in the word “washing,” and a room like this one is the kind of place where baptisms were later done. 1 Peter 3:21 says that “the baptism that now saves you” is not a bath for the body but “the pledge of a clear conscience toward God.” The basin at Dura-Europos is the oldest known Christian baptistery.
c: It is about 180 years later than Romans, and in Syria rather than Rome. It shows the form a house church could take, not how the Roman churches of Paul’s day met.

n: Santa Prisca on the Aventine
per: Church from the 5th century AD, on earlier buildings
w: A church on the Aventine Hill built over Roman houses and a shrine of Mithras. A medieval tradition says it stands on the house where Priscilla and Aquila hosted a church.
m: Paul greets “Prisca and Aquila” and “the church that meets at their house” (Romans 16:3-5). Romans does not say where in Rome they lived. Second Timothy 4:19 greets “Prisca and Aquila,” who appear to be back in the east. The church of Santa Prisca stands where a tradition places their house, but the tradition is late.
c: There is no evidence behind the tradition. The church is named for a martyr called Prisca, who may be a different person, and the link with Paul’s friend is a later guess.

n: The names in Romans 16 and the households of Rome
pl: Catacomb of Domitilla, Rome, and other Roman burials
w: Many of the names Paul greets (Ampliatus, Urbanus, Tryphaena, Hermes, Julia) appear in Roman inscriptions, often for slaves and freed people. An early tomb in the Domitilla catacomb carries the name Ampliatus. Narcissus, whose household Paul greets, was a powerful freedman of Claudius, forced to die in AD 54.
m: The list in Romans 16 reads like the people of a real city: slaves, freed people, workers and a few with money. It shows that the church in Rome reached down into households of every rank.
c: The tomb of Ampliatus may or may not be the man of Romans 16:8, since the name was common. “Household of Aristobulus” has been linked with a relative of Herod, but that is a guess.

n: The customs law of Asia
w: A long Greek inscription that sets out the duties on goods entering the province of Asia and the rules for the tax collectors who gathered them.
m: In Romans 13:6-7 Paul tells the believers to pay “taxes to whom taxes are due, revenue to whom revenue is due.” The Greek words (phoros for direct tax, telos for customs duty) match the two main kinds of Roman charge. The inscription shows how detailed and hated the system of customs collection was.
c: The inscription is from Asia and dates a few years after Romans. Tacitus (Annals 13.50-51) says that in AD 58 complaints about tax collectors in Rome itself were loud enough for Nero to consider ending the indirect taxes.

n: Coins of the young Nero and Agrippina
pl: Rome mint; examples in museums across Europe
w: Gold and silver coins from Nero’s first years show him and his mother Agrippina face to face, with her name on the front. Later coins drop her.
m: Romans 13 was written under this young emperor, in the early years of his rule when his advisers kept order. The coins show the empire Paul spoke about. If Paul wrote 1 Timothy in the 60s, the “king” and “those in authority” of 1 Timothy 2:1-2 would include Nero, who ruled from AD 54 to 68. Coins like these show how the emperor was shown to the public. Early Christian writers place Paul’s death under Nero, who ruled from AD 54 to 68, so these coins show the ruler under whom he is said to have died. 1 Peter 2:13-17 tells the readers to submit to “the king as the supreme authority” and to “honor the king.” The king in the early 60s was Nero, whose coins and portraits were in every town of the provinces.
c: The coins date the setting, not Paul’s meaning. Persecution under Nero began in AD 64, after Romans was written, and Paul does not mention it.

n: Grafting olive trees
pl: Olive groves around Jerusalem and the Mediterranean
w: Farmers have grown olives by grafting for thousands of years. A cultivated olive gives good oil but needs a vigorous rootstock. The Roman writer Columella (about AD 60s) describes grafting wild olive shoots into an old tree to renew it.
m: Paul says the Gentile believers are like “a wild olive shoot” that has “been grafted in among the others” (Romans 11:17). He notes that this is “contrary to nature,” and that the natural branches can be grafted in again (11:23-24). James 3:12 asks, “can a fig tree grow olives, or a grapevine bear figs?” A good olive oil comes from a cultivated olive, so a farmer knew that a tree bears its own fruit, and grafting a wild shoot (Romans 11) is the exception that proves how unusual it is.
c: Scholars debate whether Paul’s picture matches the farming practice of his day. He may be choosing an unusual picture on purpose.

n: Potters’ kilns of the Roman period
w: Excavations show clay pits, kilns and drying yards where jars and bowls were made. A potter shaped each vessel on a wheel from clay dug nearby.
m: Paul asks whether the potter has the right “to make from the same lump of clay one vessel for special occasions and another for common use” (Romans 9:21), echoing Isaiah 29:16 and Jeremiah 18. His readers knew potters at work. In 2 Corinthians 4:7 Paul says, “we have this treasure in jars of clay to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us.”
c: The kilns at Qumran are one example; scholars debate the purpose of the site as a whole. The Bible’s potter pictures also do not settle the debate over election.

n: The market at Pompeii
w: A covered meat and fish market beside the Forum, with a central shrine and stalls round a courtyard. Part of the meat sold in such markets had been offered in temple sacrifices.
m: In Romans 14 some believers eat anything and others eat only vegetables, and Paul says not to judge each other over food (14:1-3, 14-15, 20-21). A Roman market shows why: meat could be tied to temple sacrifice, and a careful believer might avoid it.
c: Pompeii is a Roman town in Italy and not Rome itself. Paul does not mention idol meat in Romans 14, though he does in 1 Corinthians 8-10.

n: Tarraco and the road to Spain
w: Tarraco was the capital of the Roman province of Hispania Tarraconensis. It stood on the Via Augusta, the coast road that ran from the Pyrenees to Gades (Cádiz). Walls, a circus, an amphitheater and a forum survive.
m: Paul tells the Romans that he hopes to visit them on his way to Spain (Romans 15:24, 28) and that he wants their help for the journey. Spain was the western edge of the empire, far from the places where Paul had worked.
c: Most of the visible Roman ruins in Tarragona are later than Paul. Romans does not name any city in Spain, so Tarraco is only a likely first stop.

n: Salona and Illyricum
w: Salona was the capital of the Roman province of Dalmatia, part of Illyricum on the Adriatic coast. Its walls, forum, amphitheater and early Christian basilicas have been excavated.
m: Paul says, “from Jerusalem all the way around to Illyricum, I have fully proclaimed the gospel of Christ” (Romans 15:19). Acts does not mention Illyricum, and Paul may be describing the western edge of his work in Macedonia. 2 Timothy 4:10 says Titus went to Dalmatia. Salona was the main city of Dalmatia, where 2 Timothy 4:10 says Titus had gone. The letter names only the region. Titus 3:12 asks Titus to join Paul at Nicopolis, and 2 Timothy 4:10 says Titus later went to Dalmatia. Dalmatia was part of the older region of Illyricum, which Paul names in Romans 15:19.
c: Nothing links Paul himself to Salona. The Christian remains there are from the following centuries.

n: Mamre, near Hebron
w: A large rectangular enclosure of fitted stones built in the time of Herod stands around a spot that Jews and Christians have long linked with Abraham’s oak. Later Roman and Byzantine builders added a market and a church.
m: Paul uses Abraham as his main example of faith being counted as righteousness (Romans 4:1-5, quoting Genesis 15:6) and as father of all who believe (4:11-12, 16-18). Genesis places Abraham living at Mamre in the years of the promise (Genesis 13:18; 18:1). In Galatians 3 Paul argues from Abraham: “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (3:6), and the promise came 430 years before the law (3:17). Hebrews 11:9 says that Abraham lived in tents in the land of promise, and Genesis puts his tents at Mamre. The saying in 13:2, that some have entertained angels without knowing it, recalls his meal with three visitors at Mamre (Genesis 18). James 2:23 says Abraham “was called a friend of God.” The name of Hebron in Arabic, al-Khalil, means “the friend,” and comes from the same title of Abraham.
c: The enclosure is Herodian and later, thousands of years after Abraham. The identification with the oaks of Abraham is traditional.
r: Romans 4:1-25; Genesis 13:18; Genesis 18:1; Galatians 3:6-9; Galatians 3:16-18; Hebrews 11:9-12; Hebrews 13:2; James 2:21-23

n: Ur of the Chaldeans (Tell el-Muqayyar)
w: A great temple tower (ziggurat) built about 2100 BC for the moon god Nanna, and the royal tombs and houses of the city, stand in southern Iraq. Genesis 11:31 says Abraham’s family left “Ur of the Chaldeans” for Haran and Canaan.
m: Romans 4:3 says Abraham “believed God,” even though his family came from a world of many gods (Joshua 24:2). Ur shows the setting of that world. Hebrews 11:8-10 does not name Ur. It says that Abraham went out not knowing where he was going, lived in tents, and looked for a city with foundations whose builder is God. The picture of a tent dweller who left a great city for a city to come is set against a place like Ur.
c: Some scholars place Ur of the Chaldeans elsewhere (for example in northern Mesopotamia), and the date of Abraham is debated.

n: The Alexamenos graffito
pl: Palatine Hill, Rome (now in the Palatine Museum)
w: A scratched drawing of a man with an ass’s head on a cross, and a figure raising a hand to him. The Greek caption reads, “Alexamenos worships his god.”
m: Paul writes, “I am not ashamed of the gospel” (Romans 1:16). The graffito is the earliest picture of the crucifixion we have, and it shows how the cross looked to a Roman: shameful.
c: It is more than a century after Romans, and the meaning of the drawing is debated. It does show how Christian faith was mocked in Rome.

n: The Temple of Apollo at Corinth
per: About 540 BC, standing in Paul’s day
w: A Doric temple on a rise above the forum. Seven of its limestone columns, each cut from a single block and about twenty-four feet high, still stand. It was one of the few old buildings that stayed upright after Rome destroyed the Greek city in 146 BC.
m: Paul tells the church that he “laid a foundation as an expert builder,” and that “you yourselves are God’s temple” (1 Corinthians 3:10-17). Believers in Corinth saw Greek temples every day, and Paul says they themselves are the place where God’s Spirit lives. In 2 Corinthians 6:16 he asks, “What agreement can exist between the temple of God and idols? For we are the temple of the living God.”
c: Paul does not mention this temple or any other pagan building in this passage. Its stones show what a famous temple looked like in his city, not what he had in mind.

n: The theater at Corinth
per: Greek theater rebuilt in Roman times
w: A large theater cut into the slope north of the forum, with the stone paving that carries the name of Erastus beside it. It was rebuilt by the Romans and later altered for shows with animals.
m: Paul says God “has displayed us apostles at the end of the procession, like prisoners appointed for death. We have become a spectacle to the whole world” (1 Corinthians 4:9). Readers in a theater city knew what a public spectacle was. He also writes of a “ringing gong” (13:1) and a trumpet that must give a clear call (14:8).
c: The Roman writer Vitruvius says bronze sounding vessels were placed in some theaters to carry the voice. That is one suggestion for the “gong” in 13:1, but nothing shows such vessels were used in Corinth, and the Greek word could mean other things.

n: The Bema in the forum at Corinth
w: A raised marble platform in the middle of the forum, from which magistrates could address the crowd and hear cases. Its remains stand in the center of the upper terrace.
m: Acts 18:12-17 says the Jews brought Paul “before the judgment seat” (bema) of Gallio. Paul then asks why believers take quarrels “before the unrighteous instead of before the saints” (1 Corinthians 6:1-8), in the same city where he had seen how a court worked. In 2 Corinthians 5:10 he uses the same word for a higher court: “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.”
c: Much of the surviving platform is later than Paul, and scholars disagree on how much of it was standing in AD 51-52. The site shows the kind of place where cases were heard but cannot be tied to Gallio’s hearing.

n: Acrocorinth and the Temple of Aphrodite
per: Temple from the 5th century BC; Roman-era temple described about AD 170
w: A steep rock about 1,880 feet high, towering over the city and ringed by medieval walls. Foundations of a temple of Aphrodite lie on the summit. Pausanias, writing around AD 170, describes the temple and its statue of the goddess.
m: Paul writes “Flee from sexual immorality” and tells the Corinthians that their body “is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you” (1 Corinthians 6:12-20). Corinth had a reputation for sexual excess, and the hill was the city’s most visible sign of Aphrodite.
c: Strabo says the old temple had over a thousand temple slaves, but he is describing the Greek city that Rome destroyed in 146 BC. Whether the Roman city had anything like it is debated, so the stories of mass temple prostitution should be read with care.

n: The Asklepieion at Corinth: a healing sanctuary with banquet halls
per: 4th century BC, used into Roman times
w: A healing sanctuary dedicated to Asklepios, with a spring, courtyards, and three dining rooms with stone couches along the walls where worshipers ate in the god’s precinct. Thousands of clay offerings in the shape of body parts were left there.
m: Paul asks the Corinthians about eating “in an idol’s temple” (1 Corinthians 8:10) and warns that “you cannot partake in the table of the Lord and the table of demons too” (10:21). Dining rooms like these were where meals in a god’s honor were held, and the meal could be a social event for the whole city. In 2 Corinthians 12:7-9 Paul says he pleaded three times for his thorn in the flesh to be taken away, and the answer was “My grace is sufficient for you.” People at healing sanctuaries like this one left clay models of the part that hurt, but Paul’s prayer received a different answer.
c: Paul does not name any temple, and the dining rooms of Demeter and Kore on the slope of Acrocorinth are also candidates. These excavations show the kind of meal Paul had in mind, not a place he is known to have visited.

n: The meat market of Corinth
w: A market building near the forum with a courtyard and rooms for shops. Butchers and food sellers worked here. Much of the meat offered in a Roman city came from animals killed in temple sacrifices, with the priests keeping a share and selling the rest.
m: Paul tells believers, “Eat anything sold in the meat market without raising questions of conscience” (1 Corinthians 10:25). The Greek word is makellon, the same as the Latin macellum borrowed into Greek.
c: Which building at Corinth was the one Paul meant is an inference from the layout and finds. The point is that a shopper in Corinth could buy meat without knowing where it had been offered.

n: The shops of the forum at Corinth
w: Rows of small shops opened onto the forum and the main road to the harbor at Lechaion. Many were small rooms with a counter at the front, where workers made and sold goods.
m: Acts 18:3 says Paul stayed and worked with Aquila and Priscilla because they were tentmakers. Paul tells the Corinthians that he had the right to be paid but did not use it, so as not to “hinder the gospel of Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:12, 15-18). In 2 Corinthians 11:7 he reminds them that he preached “free of charge,” and in 5:1 he calls the body an “earthly tent,” a picture from his own trade. In both Thessalonian letters Paul says he worked “night and day” so as not to burden anyone (1 Thessalonians 2:9; 2 Thessalonians 3:8). He kept his trade in Corinth with Aquila and Priscilla (Acts 18:3), and the shops of a Greek city were the sort of place where such work was done.
c: The shops show what a craftsman’s working life looked like. Nothing identifies the shop where Paul worked.
r: Acts 18:1-4; 1 Corinthians 9:3-18; 2 Corinthians 5:1-4; 2 Corinthians 11:7-9; 1 Thessalonians 2:9; 2 Thessalonians 3:8

n: Lead curse tablets from Corinth
pl: Sanctuary of Demeter and Kore, Acrocorinth; Corinth museum
per: 4th century BC to the Roman period
w: Thin sheets of lead scratched with names and curses, rolled up and left in a sanctuary on the slope of Acrocorinth. They ask the gods below to harm named enemies.
m: Paul tells the church to “hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved” (1 Corinthians 5:5), and warns that “the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons” (10:20). The tablets show that cursing and fear of unseen powers were part of everyday religion in Corinth. Paul lists “hatred, discord, jealousy, and rage; rivalries, divisions, factions, and envy” among the acts of the flesh (Galatians 5:20-21). Tablets like these show hatred put into writing against a named rival.
c: Paul’s words in 5:5 are a church decision about a member, not a curse formula, and scholars differ on what he means. The tablets give background only.

n: Isthmia: the sanctuary of Poseidon and the Isthmian Games
per: Games from 582 BC; running in Paul’s day
w: A sanctuary of Poseidon on the narrow strip of land between the Corinthian and Saronic gulfs, about ten miles from Corinth. Excavations show the temple, a stadium with a starting line, and the remains of the baths and shrines around them.
m: Paul writes, “Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize?” and speaks of a crown “that is perishable” against one “that is imperishable” (1 Corinthians 9:24-27). The Isthmian Games, held every two years, were one of the four great Greek festivals. Philippians 3:13-14 pictures a runner “straining toward what is ahead” who presses “toward the goal to win the prize.” Paul lived in Corinth for a year and a half (Acts 18:11), about ten miles from the stadium at Isthmia. Second Timothy 2:5 says that a competitor “does not receive the crown unless he competes according to the rules,” and in 4:7-8 Paul says, “I have finished the race,” and looks for “the crown of righteousness.” The Isthmian Games gave their winners a wreath of leaves. Hebrews 12:1 asks the readers to run with endurance the race set out for them, throwing off every encumbrance. The picture of a runner in a stadium would be familiar from games like those at Isthmia.
c: The winner’s wreath was of pine or celery, and ancient writers disagree about which was used when. Paul does not mention Isthmia by name, and much of what is visible today, such as the Roman baths, is later than his day.

n: Delphi: the oracle of Apollo
per: Oracle active from about the 8th century BC to the 4th century AD
w: The temple of Apollo, built into the slope of Mount Parnassus. A priestess called the Pythia gave answers in the inner room, and priests shaped them into replies. Over the entrance were sayings such as “Know yourself.”
m: Paul asks, “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the philosopher of this age?” (1 Corinthians 1:20). He reminds the Corinthians that when they were pagans they were “led astray to mute idols” (12:2), and he asks that speech in tongues be interpreted (14:27-28). Delphi is about forty-five miles from Corinth across the gulf, and many people in Corinth had consulted it.
c: Ancient writers describe the Pythia in a state of trance, but scholars debate what really happened. Greek oracles and the speaking in tongues in Corinth are not the same thing, and Paul does not compare them.

n: Delphi: slaves “sold” to Apollo for freedom
pl: Polygonal wall, sanctuary of Apollo, Delphi, Greece
per: Mostly 2nd century BC to 1st century AD
w: More than a thousand inscriptions cut into the sanctuary walls record slaves being freed. In the usual form the slave pays the master a price, and the god Apollo “buys” the slave for freedom, so the slave belongs to the god and cannot be taken back.
m: Paul writes, “You were bought at a price” (1 Corinthians 6:20; 7:23) and “he who was a slave when he was called by the Lord is the Lord’s freedman” (7:22). The inscriptions show the kind of purchase his readers knew, in which the one who buys becomes the new owner. In Galatians 4:5 Christ came “to redeem those under the law,” and 5:1 says “It is for freedom that Christ has set us free.” The Greek verb for “redeem” is the same word as buying, as in these sales to the god. Ephesians 1:7 says “In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses,” and 4:30 looks ahead to “the day of redemption.” The word for redemption is the language of buying a person out of slavery. Colossians 3:11 says “Christ is all and is in all,” and so there is no difference between slave and free. Colossians 4:1 tells masters that “you also have a Master in heaven.” First Timothy 6:1-2 shows slaves and masters together in the church. Inscriptions like these show that some slaves could buy their freedom, though the letter does not say whether this was the case for slaves in the church. Philemon 15-16 asks Philemon to have Onesimus back “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother,” and verse 21 says he will do “even more than I ask.” Some readers hear a hint of freedom. Inscriptions like these show how freedom was recorded in Paul’s day, but the letter does not use the language of release.
c: Paul does not mention Delphi, and not every Corinthian would have thought of this practice. The inscriptions illustrate the language but do not show that he was using this custom.
r: 1 Corinthians 6:19-20; 1 Corinthians 7:21-23; Galatians 3:13; Galatians 4:5; Galatians 5:1; Ephesians 1:7; Ephesians 4:30; Colossians 3:11; Colossians 4:1; 1 Timothy 6:1-2; Philemon 1:15-16; Philemon 1:21

n: Everyday Greek letters on papyrus
pl: Oxyrhynchus and other Egyptian sites (collections in Oxford, London and elsewhere)
w: Thousands of private letters on papyrus survive from Egypt. They open with the sender, the reader, and a greeting, often add thanks to the gods and a wish for health, pass on news, send greetings by name, and end with a farewell.
m: Paul’s letters follow this pattern with changes of his own: “grace and peace” in place of the usual greeting, and thanksgiving for the church. In 1 Corinthians he answers a letter (7:1), reports what visitors have told him (1:11), and ends with greetings and a note in his own hand (16:19-21). Surviving papyri include letters of recommendation, which introduced travelers to people who did not know them. In 2 Corinthians Paul asks whether he needs “letters of recommendation” (3:1), recalls a sharp letter that “caused you sorrow” (7:8), and answers critics who say “His letters are weighty and forceful” (10:10). In Galatians 6:11 Paul writes, “See what large letters I am using to write to you with my own hand!” Papyrus letters were often dictated to a scribe, and the sender sometimes added the last lines in his own hand. Ephesians 6:21-22 says “Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord, will tell you everything.” A letter was often carried and explained by a trusted messenger, who could add what the page left out. Philippians 2:25 calls Epaphroditus “your messenger and minister to my needs,” and in 4:18 Paul writes, “I have all I need and more, now that I have received your gifts.” The Greek for “I have received” (apecho) was the usual word on papyrus receipts, where it meant “paid in full.” Colossians 4:18 says “This greeting is in my own hand—Paul.” On papyrus letters a scribe often wrote the body and the sender added the last line himself. Colossians 4:16 also shows letters being read aloud to a church and then passed on. First Thessalonians 5:27 tells the church to have the letter “read to all the brothers.” Second Thessalonians 3:17 says “This greeting is in my own hand—Paul. This is my mark in every letter,” which fits the way a scribe wrote the body of a letter and the sender added the last line. Philemon opens as ordinary letters did, with sender, reader, greeting and thanks (verses 1-7). In verse 19 Paul says, “I, Paul, write this with my own hand,” and promises to repay, much as a person signed a note of debt. James opens as an ordinary Greek letter did: the sender, the readers, and the plain greeting chairein (“Greetings”). Paul replaces that greeting with “grace and peace,” so the opening is one of the things that sets James apart. 1 Peter opens with the sender, the readers and the greeting “Grace and peace be yours in abundance,” and closes with greetings from “Silvanus,” who may have been the scribe or the courier. In the letters on papyrus, a person who wrote for another could be named at the close. 2 John 12 says the writer would rather not write with “paper and ink” but speak face to face, and 3 John 13 says “pen and ink.” A sheet of papyrus and soot-and-gum ink were the everyday tools of the Greek letters found in Egypt, and a letter of about 245 Greek words, as 2 John is, fits on one sheet. 3 John is the New Testament book closest in size and shape to an everyday papyrus letter: the names, a wish for health (verse 2), the business in hand, a hope to visit, and greetings to friends (verses 13-14). At about 219 Greek words it would fit on one sheet.
c: The papyri come from Egypt, not Greece, and most are from ordinary people rather than leaders. They show how letters were written in his day and not how any one of them worked.
r: 1 Corinthians 1:1-9; 1 Corinthians 16:19-24; 2 Corinthians 3:1-3; 2 Corinthians 7:8-12; 2 Corinthians 10:9-11; 2 Corinthians 13:10; Galatians 1:1-5; Galatians 6:11; Ephesians 6:21-22; Philippians 2:25; Philippians 4:18; Colossians 4:16; Colossians 4:18; 1 Thessalonians 5:27; 2 Thessalonians 3:17; Philemon 1:1-7; Philemon 1:19; James 1:1; 1 Peter 1:1; 1 Peter 5:12; 2 John 12; 3 John 13; 3 John 2; 3 John 13-14

n: The house church at Dura-Europos
w: An ordinary house in a Roman border town that was rebuilt to serve as a church. The wall between two rooms was removed to make a larger meeting room, and a small room with a basin was painted with scenes from the Gospels as a baptistery.
m: Paul wrote to a church that met in homes (1 Corinthians 11:18-22; 14:26; 16:19). The Dura house shows what a house looks like when it becomes a meeting place, and how many it could hold. Colossians 4:15 greets Nympha and “the church that meets at her house,” and Philemon 2 speaks of “the church that meets at your house.” These were the places where the churches of the Lycus Valley gathered. First Timothy 3:15 speaks of “God’s household, which is the church of the living God.” The house church at Dura-Europos is much later than Paul, in the AD 230s, but it shows how a private house could be changed for the church to meet in. Philemon 2 greets “the church that meets at your house,” so the church at Colossae, or part of it, gathered in a private home. The Dura house shows a family home turned into a place for worship, a century and a half after 2 John, where the “home” of verse 10 was the place where a church met and where travelers were lodged. In 3 John the church meets in homes too: Diotrephes can keep the brothers out and put people “out of the church” (verse 10), which is easiest to picture if the meeting was under his roof.
c: It dates roughly 180 to 200 years after Paul. It is the earliest house church known, but not a church of his time, and in Corinth the church may have used larger homes of its wealthier members.
r: 1 Corinthians 11:17-34; 1 Corinthians 14:26-33; 1 Corinthians 16:19; Colossians 4:15; 1 Timothy 3:15; Philemon 1:2; 2 John 10-11; 3 John 9-10

n: Veiled heads in Roman art
pl: Statues of Augustus and of Roman women (Rome, Corinth and elsewhere)
w: Statues show Roman men and women with a fold of the toga or a veil drawn over the head. The best-known is Augustus as high priest, his toga pulled over his head as he leads a sacrifice. Portraits of women in Corinth and across the empire show veils as well.
m: Paul says “Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head,” and “every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head” (1 Corinthians 11:4-5). Covering the head in prayer was a Roman custom for men at sacrifices, so Paul’s instruction would have seemed odd to a Roman reader.
c: Customs about head coverings differed from city to city and from class to class, and scholars still debate exactly what Paul meant in 11:2-16. The statues show habits of the time, not an answer to the debate.

n: Clay body parts left at healing sanctuaries
pl: Corinth Asklepieion and other Greek sanctuaries
per: 5th century BC to the Roman period
w: Clay models of hands, feet, eyes, ears, arms and other body parts were left at healing sanctuaries by people who had been cured or who hoped to be. Thousands came from the Asklepieion at Corinth.
m: Paul says “The body is a unit, though it is composed of many parts,” and goes on to speak of the foot, the hand, the ear and the eye (1 Corinthians 12:12-21). In Corinth these were familiar pictures, because worshipers gave models of single body parts to their god.
c: Paul does not mention the offerings. The comparison is one we draw, not one the letter makes.

n: Bronze mirrors
pl: Museums in Greece and elsewhere (Corinth was known for its bronze work)
per: 5th century BC to the 1st century AD
w: Mirrors in Paul’s day were disks of polished bronze, sometimes with decorated handles. They gave a darker and less exact image than glass. The Roman writer Pliny says Corinthian bronze was prized across the empire.
m: Paul writes, “Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12). A reader in Corinth, known for its bronze work, would have looked into such a mirror. In 2 Corinthians 3:18 Paul says believers “with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord.” The Greek verb can also mean to look as in a mirror, and a reader in Corinth knew mirrors well. James 1:23-24 compares a person who hears the word and does not act to a man who looks at his face in a mirror and forgets what he looked like. The Greek word for mirror (esoptron) occurs only here and in 1 Corinthians 13:12. A mirror of polished metal gave a dim image, so the picture is of a quick and imperfect glance.
c: Pliny wrote after Paul and mixes legend with fact about “Corinthian bronze.” The point is only that metal mirrors, which show a blurred image, were the common kind.

n: The gladiator cemetery at Ephesus
w: A burial ground found in 1993 holding the bones of about sixty-seven men, most of them young and strong, with injuries from blades and clubs. One bone is reported to show the bite of a large cat.
m: Paul asks, “If I fought wild beasts in Ephesus for human motives, what did I gain?” (1 Corinthians 15:32). Ephesus had an arena in which animals and fighters were used for shows, so the picture was one his readers could imagine. Hebrews 10:32-34 recalls a time when the readers were publicly abused and afflicted. The writer does not say what form it took, but public shaming in the arena or street was a common form of punishment in the Roman world.
c: These burials are about a century after Paul, and Paul may be speaking in a figure of speech: a Roman citizen was not normally thrown to beasts, and Acts does not describe such a scene. The graves show the arena culture of the city, not an event in his life.

n: Clay seals and deposit receipts
pl: Jerusalem (clay seals); Oxyrhynchus and other Egyptian sites (papyri)
per: Seals from the 8th century BC on; papyri from Roman Egypt
w: Excavations in Jerusalem have turned up many small lumps of clay stamped with a seal, used to close a document or a jar. One found in the Ophel in 2009 bears the name of King Hezekiah. Papyrus contracts and receipts from Egypt use the Greek word arrabon for a down payment that guarantees the rest will be paid.
m: Paul writes that God “placed His seal on us, and put His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge of what is to come” (2 Corinthians 1:22). A seal showed who owned something, and a pledge was a first payment that promised the rest. Paul uses both pictures of the Spirit, and again in 5:5. Ephesians 1:13-14 says believers “were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the pledge of our inheritance,” and 4:30 says “you were sealed for the day of redemption.” The same two ideas of ownership and a first payment appear here.
c: The Hezekiah seal and the papyri come from different places and centuries, and none is from Corinth. They show how seals and deposits worked, not what Paul saw.

n: The triumph on the Arch of Titus
per: Built after AD 81; shows the triumph of AD 71
w: A marble arch at the edge of the Forum, built after Titus died in AD 81. Panels inside the passage show soldiers carrying the gold lampstand and other spoils from the temple through Rome, and the emperor riding in a four-horse chariot.
m: Paul writes that God “always leads us triumphantly as captives in Christ and through us spreads everywhere the fragrance of the knowledge of Him” (2 Corinthians 2:14). A Roman triumph was the victorious general’s parade through the city, with captives walking in it. Scholars disagree whether Paul sees himself as a captive or as a soldier in the procession. Colossians 2:15 says that God, “having disarmed the powers and authorities,” “made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross.” The Arch of Titus shows what such a triumph looked like, with the defeated and their spoils paraded before the crowd. Hebrews 8:13 calls the first covenant aging and soon to disappear. The Arch of Titus shows Roman soldiers carrying off the Temple’s treasures after the destruction of AD 70. Whether Hebrews was written before or after that is debated, and the letter never mentions the destruction. Rome’s destruction of Jerusalem and its temple in AD 70 is one reason John can call Rome “Babylon,” the name of the empire that destroyed the first temple (Revelation 17:5).
c: This arch was built after Paul’s death and marks the fall of Jerusalem. It shows what a triumph looked like, not a scene Paul saw.
r: 2 Corinthians 2:14-16; Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 8:13; Hebrews 10:11; Revelation 11:1-2; Revelation 17:5

n: The Res Gestae of Augustus at Ankara
pl: Temple of Roma and Augustus, Ankara, Turkey
w: The walls of a temple of Rome and Augustus in Ankara carry the Latin and Greek text of the emperor’s own account of his deeds, copied from bronze tablets in Rome after his death in AD 14. It lists wars won, money spent, buildings raised, and kings and peoples who sent ambassadors to him.
m: Paul writes “we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making His appeal through us,” and says God was “reconciling the world to Himself in Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:19-20). In the Roman world an ambassador carried the word of a ruler who was not present, and the emperor’s own inscription boasts of peoples who sent ambassadors to him. Ankara was ancient Ancyra, a leading city of the Roman province of Galatia. Another copy of the same text was found at Pisidian Antioch, in the south of the province. Ankara (ancient Ancyra) was the capital of the Roman province of Galatia, one of the five named in 1 Peter 1:1. It is the pin used on the map for the readers of the letter.
c: The inscription is a copy made soon after Augustus died, decades before Paul’s letter, and Paul does not mention it. It shows the language of the empire, not a source for his words.

n: The Roman siege ramp at Masada
w: Rome besieged Masada after the war of AD 66-70, building a wall around the cliff, camps for the besieging troops, and a huge ramp of earth and stone against the western side. The ramp and the camps are still visible.
m: Paul says “we do not wage war according to the flesh. The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the world. Instead, they have divine power to demolish strongholds” (2 Corinthians 10:3-4). His readers knew how armies took strongholds with ramps and siege engines, and Paul says his weapons work on arguments and thoughts.
c: The siege was after Paul’s death and was a Roman war on Jewish rebels. It shows how a stronghold was taken, not anything Paul saw in Corinth.

n: The Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice
pl: Qumran caves; another copy found at Masada
per: Copied in the 1st century BC to the 1st century AD
w: Fragments of thirteen songs for thirteen Sabbaths describe angels praising God in a heavenly temple. Copies were found at Qumran and at Masada.
m: Paul writes of a man who “was caught up to the third heaven” and then to “Paradise,” where he heard “things that man is not permitted to tell” (2 Corinthians 12:2-4). Some Jewish writers of his day described visits to the heavens, and these songs show that a heavenly temple was a live idea. Colossians 1:16 names “thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities,” and 2:18 speaks of “the worship of angels.” These songs show Jews of Paul’s time picturing angels who praise God in a heavenly temple, so the idea of an angelic liturgy was alive. Whether the teachers at Colossae knew anything like it is not known. Hebrews pictures a heavenly sanctuary, and it ends with the angels in festal gathering around the city of the living God (12:22-23). The Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice describe angelic priests serving in heavenly temples, so the idea of a heavenly sanctuary was familiar to Jews of the time.
c: The songs do not mention a third heaven or Paradise, and nothing says Paul knew them. They show only that heavenly worship was a subject among Jews of his time.

n: The Celts of Galatia
pl: Central Anatolia around Ankara, Pessinus and Tavium, Turkey
per: Settled from 278-277 BC; Roman province from 25 BC
w: Celtic tribes crossed from Europe into Anatolia in 278-277 BC and settled in the central plateau. Greeks called them Galatai, the same word as “Gauls.” Pergamum and then Rome defeated them, and in 25 BC Augustus made a Roman province of Galatia that took in their old land and also reached south to cities such as Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe.
m: Paul writes “to the churches of Galatia” (Galatians 1:2) and calls his readers “foolish Galatians” (3:1). Scholars disagree about where they lived. One view says they were in the old Celtic north, the other says they were in the Roman province’s southern cities that Paul reached in Acts 13-14. Both views fit the word “Galatian.” Second Timothy 4:10 says Crescens “has gone to Galatia.” Some early manuscripts read “Gaul” instead, and the two Greek names are close. The Celts of Galatia were Gauls who had settled in central Asia Minor about 278 BC. Galatia is the second of the five provinces named in 1 Peter 1:1, after Pontus. The province was a mixture of Celts, Greeks, Jews and Roman colonists.
c: The letter names no city in Galatia, so this entry cannot say which view is right. Later writers say people in the north kept a Celtic language for centuries, but that is not in Paul’s letter.

n: Jebel Musa: the traditional Mount Sinai
per: Christian tradition from about the 4th century
w: A granite peak of about 2,285 meters in the south of the Sinai Peninsula. By the 4th century Christian visitors and monks were pointing to it as the mountain where Moses received the law, and the monastery of St Catherine now stands at its foot.
m: Paul writes that “Hagar stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia” (Galatians 4:25). He places Sinai in Arabia and ties it to the law given there, which he sets beside the free “Jerusalem above” (4:26). Hebrews 12:18-21 recalls the scene at Sinai, with a blazing fire, darkness, a trumpet and a voice so terrifying that the people begged not to hear more. It contrasts that mountain with Mount Zion, and Jebel Musa is only one of several places proposed for Sinai. 1 Peter 2:9 gives the church the titles God gave Israel at Sinai: “a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (Exodus 19:5-6). Jebel Musa is the traditional Sinai, though the site is debated.
c: The Bible does not fix the location of Mount Sinai, and several other mountains have been proposed. This is the mountain Christian tradition has long named, not one proven by excavation.

n: The pedagogue and the schoolboy
pl: Greek vases and Roman reliefs in museums in Europe
per: Greek vase paintings from the 5th century BC; Roman reliefs and texts
w: Greek vase paintings and Roman reliefs show boys at lessons with an older man standing or sitting near. He is the paidagogos, usually a trusted slave who walked a child to school and back, carried his things, watched his manners and could punish him. He taught no lessons, and his duties ended when the boy came of age.
m: Paul says “the law became our guardian to lead us to Christ” and “now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian” (Galatians 3:24-25). The Greek word for “guardian” is paidagogos. Paul uses the picture of a minder who is in charge for a time and then steps aside.
c: The scenes come from many places and centuries, and none is from Galatia. They show what the role looked like, but Paul’s point about the law is argued in his own words and scholars discuss how negative or positive the picture is.

n: The Via Sebaste: Augustus’ road in southern Galatia
pl: Between Pisidian Antioch and Lystra, Turkey
w: Augustus’ governor in the province of Galatia had a road built about 6 BC to join the new Roman colonies of the south, including Pisidian Antioch and Lystra. Milestones along it carry the emperor’s name, and stretches of paving survive.
m: Acts 13-14 follows Paul and Barnabas through Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, and some scholars think the “churches of Galatia” (Galatians 1:2) were these southern churches. Paul says he first preached to them “because of an illness” (4:13), and it is easy to picture a traveler held up on a road like this one.
c: Acts does not name this road, and the milestones say nothing of Paul. The entry fits only the southern view of where the Galatians lived, which not all scholars accept.

n: The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran
pl: Shrine of the Book, Jerusalem (found in Qumran Cave 1)
per: Copied about the late 1st century BC
w: A scroll found in Cave 1 in 1947 quotes the prophet Habakkuk a line at a time and explains each line as pointing to the community’s own day. The explanation of Habakkuk 2:4, “the righteous will live by his faith,” says it concerns those who keep the law, whom God will save because of their faithfulness to the community’s Teacher.
m: Paul uses the same verse: “no one is justified before God by the law, because ’The righteous will live by faith’” (Galatians 3:11). The scroll shows that Jews of his time were already reading Habakkuk 2:4 as a key verse, and that they could link “faith” to trust in a person. Paul connects it to Christ.
c: The scroll is a Jewish community text that does not mention Jesus or Paul. It shows that the verse was in use, not that Paul knew this commentary.

n: Papyrus 46: the oldest copy of Ephesians
pl: Chester Beatty Library, Dublin (some leaves at the University of Michigan)
per: About AD 200 (some scholars date it earlier)
w: A book of Paul’s letters written on papyrus, found in Egypt in the early 1930s. In it Ephesians stands after 2 Corinthians and before Galatians. It is the oldest surviving copy of the letter.
m: Many English Bibles read Ephesians 1:1 as “To the saints in Ephesus.” In this papyrus, and in the first writing of the great 4th-century Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, the words “in Ephesus” are missing. Some scholars take this as a sign that the letter went to several churches in Asia, with the place left open. Others think the words were simply dropped. The letter itself gives no other greeting to any named person. The same book holds Colossians, after Philippians. Colossians 4:16 asks the church to pass its letter on and to read “the letter from Laodicea,” which is how Paul’s letters came to be gathered into books like this one. In Papyrus 46, Hebrews comes right after Romans, which shows that Christians in Egypt in the early 200s (some scholars date the manuscript earlier) copied it with Paul’s letters. That placement is evidence of how the letter was read, not of who wrote it. 2 Peter 3:15-16 says that Paul wrote to the readers and that his letters, with “the rest of the Scriptures,” are being distorted by the unstable. A papyrus book like this one shows Paul’s letters already gathered in one volume by about AD 200.
c: No manuscript settles the matter, and most later manuscripts do have “in Ephesus.” Tertullian says the heretic Marcion called the letter “To the Laodiceans,” but that is a report about one man’s edition.

n: Laodicea on the Lycus
per: Founded in the 3rd century BC; rebuilt after an earthquake in AD 60
w: A large Roman-period city in the Lycus Valley, with a stadium, two theaters, a main street lined with columns and a water system. Clay pipes there are thickly crusted with limestone from the hard water. Excavation by a Turkish university team has been under way since 2003.
m: Colossians 4:16 tells its readers to read “the letter from Laodicea” and to make sure their own letter is read in the church at Laodicea. Tychicus carries both Colossians and Ephesians (Colossians 4:7-8; Ephesians 6:21-22). A few scholars have wondered whether “the letter from Laodicea” is Ephesians, which some of the oldest copies address to no named city. Revelation 3:14-22 later speaks to the church here. Paul says he is struggling for “those at Laodicea” (2:1) and sends greetings to “the brothers in Laodicea, as well as Nympha and the church that meets at her house” (4:15). The Roman historian Tacitus writes that Laodicea fell to an earthquake in Nero’s reign and was rebuilt with its own money (Annals 14.27), which puts the disaster near the date of the letter. In Revelation 3:14-22 the church says, “I am rich; I have grown wealthy and need nothing,” and is told that it is “lukewarm—neither hot nor cold.” Excavations since 2003 have traced the aqueduct and the stone pipes, thick with lime, that brought the city its water from springs several kilometers away; the hot pools of Hierapolis can be seen across the valley.
c: Colossians does not say what the letter from Laodicea was, and it may be lost. The link to Ephesians is a suggestion, not something the text states.

n: Colossae: the mound in the Lycus Valley
per: Prosperous in the 5th century BC; smaller by Paul’s day
w: A large, grass-covered mound with a few scattered stones beside the modern village of Honaz. The Roman city lies mostly unexcavated. Ancient writers speak of Colossae as a once-wealthy wool town that had been outgrown by nearby Laodicea and Hierapolis.
m: Tychicus is sent with Onesimus, “who is one of you,” to the Colossians (Colossians 4:7-9), and the same Tychicus carries the letter to the Ephesians (Ephesians 6:21-22). The mound shows how small and quiet a town can be that received a letter from Paul. The letter is addressed to the church here (1:2). Paul says that many “have not met me face to face” (2:1) and that Epaphras, who “is one of you,” works for the churches of Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis (4:12-13). A Turkish university team began a survey of the site in 2021 and started excavation in 2025. Philemon most likely lived at Colossae. Archippus is greeted in both Colossians 4:17 and Philemon 2, and Onesimus is “one of you” in Colossians 4:9. Verse 2 greets “the church that meets at your house,” so part of the church at Colossae may have met in Philemon’s home.
c: The letter to the Colossians is the only text that mentions the church here, and the site has produced little for the 1st century.
r: Colossians 1:1-2; Colossians 4:7-9; Philemon 1:10-12; Ephesians 6:21-22; Colossians 2:1; Colossians 4:12-13; Philemon 1:1-2; Philemon 1:10-12

n: The Terrace Houses of Ephesus
per: First built about the 1st century BC-1st century AD; lived in until about the 7th century
w: Rows of large homes on the slope across from the main street of Ephesus. Rooms open on columned courtyards, with painted walls, marble floors and mosaics, a private water supply and heating. A roof now covers them, and the Austrian team that excavated them has worked here since the 1960s.
m: Ephesians 5:21 to 6:9 speaks to the people of one household: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters.
